subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 10 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. But here is the important part for you. This is not a unit about high scores or timers; it is about two big ideas that make games work: sub-routines and repetition. The game is the joyful reason to learn them. The first big idea is the sub-routine: a set of instructions for a job you do again and again, written once and then run whenever you need it. Getting ready for school is a sub-routine — pack your bag, put on your shoes, check you have your lunch — and you do not re-learn those steps every morning; you just do the routine again. In our game, every time the player moves the cat the same little job happens (change costume, a small meow), so instead of writing it four times, once per arrow key, we write it once as Move Around. The second big idea is repetition. A forever loop repeats without ever stopping (this is repetition), while a repeat (6) loop repeats a set number of times and then stops (this is iteration, the count-controlled loop from Unit 4). In our game, a repeat loop makes the treat spin before the chase begins.

outcomes: Explain that a sub-routine is a set of instructions for a frequently-used job, made once and run many times.
In Scratch, make a sub-routine with My Blocks (Make a Block) and run it from other scripts.
Explain the difference between a forever loop (repetition — never stops) and a repeat (n) loop (iteration — a set number of times).
Recognise the event blocks that start a script: when green flag clicked, when key pressed, and when this sprite clicked.
Use coordinates to move a sprite: change x by, change y by, and glide or go to a random position.
Build a small, working game in Scratch that uses a sub-routine and a loop.
Test a program systematically — checking each part in turn — to find an error, and debug (fix) it.

concepts.title: Games repeat things: repetition and iteration
concepts.explanation:
Games are full of repeats. Some things repeat forever while you play (this is repetition); some things repeat a set number of times and then stop (this is iteration, the count-controlled loop from Unit 4).

Try it: Do the first together, then you can try the rest in pairs.

Check yourself: Can you tell a repeat that never stops (repetition, forever) from one that happens a set number of times (iteration, repeat)? Can you point to a repeat in a game?

concepts.title: Sub-routines: a job you make once and use again
concepts.explanation: A sub-routine is a set of instructions for a job used again and again. You write the steps once, give the job a name, and then run that name whenever you need it — keeping a program short and tidy. Check yourself: a job you make once and use again. Can you see why writing Move Around once is better than writing the same steps four times?

concepts.title: Add the treat: a repeat loop and click-to-catch
concepts.explanation:
Add a second sprite (the treat), use a repeat loop (iteration) for a spin animation, move it to random positions with coordinates, and make it catchable with the when this sprite clicked event and a second sub-routine.

Try it: they may change numbers and watch what happens. You add the Apple and Pop sound, build the spin (repeat loop) and the Catch Treat sub-routine, and play.

Check yourself: Are the two repeated blocks INSIDE the repeat loop (hugged by its C-shape)? Can you name the two events that start the treat's two scripts? Did you make Catch Treat in My Blocks and run it from when this sprite clicked?

debugging.symptom: A sub-routine is a brand-new kind of instruction.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Game Developer”.
debugging.fix: No — it is just a bundle of ordinary blocks you gave a name to. Nothing magic; it saves you writing the same blocks again.

debugging.symptom: Making the Move Around block runs it.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Game Developer”.
debugging.fix: No — making a block (the define hat) only creates the job. It does nothing until you drag the Move Around block into a script and run it.

debugging.symptom: repeat and forever are the same.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Game Developer”.
debugging.fix: A repeat (6) loop runs a set number of times and then stops (iteration); a forever loop never stops on its own (repetition). Count the runs together to feel the difference.

debugging.symptom: Bigger y means down, like reading down a page.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Game Developer”.
debugging.fix: On the Scratch stage, bigger y means UP and smaller y means DOWN. This is the cause of the classic down-arrow bug — worth showing slowly.

debugging.symptom: When the game misbehaves, I should delete it and start again.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Game Developer”.
debugging.fix: No — test each part in turn to find the one bug, then fix just that. Starting again usually brings the bug back.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.
